title: No miracles
text:
Empirical science rests upon a quiet leap of faith: the assumption that the universe has always operated under uniform natural laws and will continue to do so tomorrow. Yet this is an assumption, not an empirical proof.
There is no scientific guarantee that physical constants were identical a billion years ago, or that gravity will behave the same way tomorrow morning. For all we know, the cosmos could have coalesced into its present configuration moments ago, creating the grand illusion of an eternal, orderly past. No scientist, no matter how brilliant, can guarantee with absolute certainty that nature will not suddenly rewrite its rules tomorrow. True existential certainty comes not from measurement, but from the unyielding reliability of the Creator Himself!
Once God issues a decree, it does not change. Neither does anyone else has the power to change His Will. God is not a human we could watch Him do things. God’s Sunnah (behavior / way of doing things) is expressed through His creation.
But, but, but …
If the cosmos had been fashioned by a lesser deity, one might expect him to prove his majesty through theatrical displays: cooling the sun on a whim, fracturing the moon in two, or causing a steel needle to hover on water. But such demands stem from a primitive human urge for spectacle.
If a person remains uninspired by the titanic swirl of spinning galaxies, the silent majesty of black holes, and the fiery birth of stars—or by the intricate dance of subatomic quarks and invisible forces—no parlor trick will ever convince them of God’s infinite Power!
The Creator’s grand architecture is anchored in absolute Wisdom. When He endowed creation with specific attributes, He did so with perfect foresight. He designed fire with the intrinsic property to burn; He has no need to revise His original blueprint by suddenly robbing fire of its nature. Only flawed human engineers must issue patches, updates, and mid-course corrections, because human knowledge is inherently incomplete.
Through His sovereign Free Will, God chose to actualize His decrees in precise, measurable proportions — what we call the laws of nature.
He established this unwavering structure so that humanity could observe, comprehend, and harness these reliable principles for the flourishing of civilization. While God possesses the absolute power to command anything into being, He intentionally willed that His Divine Command be realized through fixed, dependable laws.

title: No miracles
text:
No Miracles for the Messenger

They say, “If only a miracle could come down to him from his Lord! @{qxp| (then we would have believed in Him.) }@” Say, “God has the Power to send down a miracle, but most of them do not use their knowledge.” [Quran 6:37]

He does not wish to stun the human intellect with supernatural phenomena. He wants believers to reflect and use reason. See [Quran 12:108]

Those who deny the truth keep saying, “Why has no miracle ever been bestowed upon him from his Lord?” But you (O Prophet) are only a warner and to every community is a guide. [Quran 13:7]


And yet they say, “Why are not miracles bestowed upon him from his Lord?” Say, “These verses are in themselves miraculous signs concerning God and with Him are the miracles (that you can see in the Universe). As for me, I am but a plain warner @{qxp| (drawing your attention to His signs and to the consequences of your actions.) }@” [Quran 29:50]


Why! Is it not enough (of a miracle) for them that We have bestowed upon you this Book that is conveyed to them? For, herein is Grace, a Reminder, and it is a giver of eminence to people who accept it. [Quran 29:51]


(Though we did not, but) Even if We had sent down to you (O Prophet) a pre-printed book written on parchment (as a miracle), so that they could feel it with their hands, the rejecters would have said, ‘This is nothing but obvious trickery!’ [Quran 6:7]

title: The Quranic God
text: When God describes His own Being, He reveals Himself as the One, Unique, and Uncaused Cause — a singular Reality without parallel anywhere in the physical cosmos or within the furthest reaches of human imagination.

title: The Quranic God
text:
One God?
God is ONE. But what does this foundational truth actually mean? God is not an object within creation that can be observed with instruments or tallied as one item among many. We perceive God through the signature of His creation. If multiple deities governed existence, each driving the cosmos according to competing desires, the universe would collapse into chaotic friction and systemic collapse. It requires no specialized degree to grasp this fundamental principle:

Had there been gods besides Allah within the heavens and earth, both would have been ruined … [Quran 21:22]

Because no secondary power exists to alter or override the cosmic order, the laws established by the One Creator remain resolute and unchanging. Yet this absolute consistency raises a profound question: does the absence of change imply that God has constrained His own Will? Has the Almighty voluntarily bound Himself to an unyielding order? Let us examine what the Quran reveals on this matter.

, “To whom belongs all that is in the heavens and earth?” Say, “To God, [Who] has prescribed for Himself grace (”mercy”) [Rahmah] …” [Quran 6:12]

He has made it “mandatory” on Himself to provide mercy [Rahmah]. He has similarly placed other restrictions on Himself.

Those who accept the Message and live upright. There is good news for them in this world and in the Hereafter. God’s Words never change … [Quran 10:63-64]

Nor does anyone else has the power to change His rules. Nor can one escape from His rules.

Completed is the Word of your Lord in truth and justice. None can change His Words. He is the Profound Hearer, the Knower. [Quran 6:115]


… None can alter His Words. And you will find no refuge other than Him. [Quran 18:27]

God is so uncompromising in His decisions, He does not deviate a bit, let alone make a complete replacement or His laws.

Nay, no change you will ever find in the Sunnah  (behavior, laws)  of God, and no deviation you will ever find in the Sunnah  (behavior, laws)  of Allah. [Quran 35:43]

God has created unwavering rules not only for the physical, but for the human life (Nafs / “soul”) and social life as well.

That was the Sunnah  (behavior, laws)  of God among those who lived before. And never will you find any change in God’s Sunnah  (behavior, laws) . [Quran 33:62]

Even a God’s messenger has no power to change any of these rules.

Messengers before you were denied and opposed … There is none to alter the Words  (Decisions, Decree)  of God … (remember they would still not believe) even if you were able to seek a tunnel in the ground or a ladder to the sky and bring them a miracle (on your own) … So, do not be among those who are swayed by ignorance  (about the free will.)  [Quran 6:34-35]

God wants His servants to reflect and make free choices. See [Quran 2:256] and [Quran 10:99]

title: The Quranic God
text:
God’s Expression [Sunnah]
We do not understand God’s actions (Sunnah) through the lens of human behavior — such as walking, talking, or eating. How, then, should we comprehend what the Quran calls “the Words of God” and His “Sunnah”?

God either talks through His messengers via His Books, or through His Creation - the universe and its laws.

His Laws in theory — the Words of God (Kalimaatillah) — and His Laws in practice as manifest throughout the cosmos — the Actions of God (Sunnatillah) — exist in flawless harmony, offering zero contradiction. Unlike human beings, whose limited foresight leads to shifting minds and revised plans, the Almighty is beyond human imperfection. Once He institutes a decree, His Will stands absolute and unyielding.
Consider how the Quran invites us to perceive His divine presence through the canvas of the observable universe:

God is the One Who causes the grains and the seeds to split and germinate (according to His Sunnah.) He produces the living from the dead, and the dead from the living. Such is God. (This is how never changing Sunnah of God works.) Where are you headed in bewilderment (looking for miracles?) [Quran 6:95]

The unyielding laws governing seed germination enable humanity to master agriculture, building civilized societies and sustaining life across millennia. If God altered the rules of germination on a whim, human civilization could never have taken root, leaving us stranded in primitive survival. Just as precise principles govern how a living plant emerges from a seemingly lifeless seed, the trajectory of human life, consciousness, and death follows an equally deliberate divine order.
This immutable structure extends far beyond Earth into the cosmic expanse. Planets, moons, and distant stars traverse paths shaped by unwavering physical laws. Were these celestial mechanics unpredictable, orbital navigation, timekeeping, and astronomical tracking would be impossible.

… (He has appointed) the sun and the moon [to run their well-calculated courses [Quran 10:5]] for calculation. [So that they become a means of calculating time for you [Quran 10:5]] . Such is the Design of the All-Powerful, the Knower. [Quran 6:96]


He is the One Who has made the stars to guide you through the darkness of the land and the sea. We have scattered Our signs [throughout the Universe] for people who use their knowledge  (about never changing natural laws) . [Quran 6:97]

Just as everything in the universe follows God’s rule, so does the evolution of life.

And He is the One Who initiated you from a single life [cell]. Then  (in the process of evolution)  He appointed stages, from one station to the next destination. (Thus, goes on the journey of life.) We explain Our Messages for people who use their insight. [Quran 6:98]

title: The Quranic God
section: Why God Cannot Have a Son?
text:
Why God Cannot Have a Son?
The cosmos itself is a majestic expression of God’s unchanging Attributes. Having established the law of biological procreation through the union of two parents, the concept of God having a literal son is incompatible with His own cosmic framework — for He has no equal nor any partner.
The divine argument is not a question of lacking creative power, but one of absolute consistency: procreation within the physical realm requires a mate, and God does not violate the immutable laws He Himself instituted. God’s Sunnah — His underlying law and conduct — remains resolute, unyielding, and forever true to its own design.

Wonderful Originator of the heavens and earth;  how can He have a son when He never chose for Himself a mate?  He creates all things (in accordance with laws) and He is the Profound Knower of all things and events. [Quran 6:101]


Did Jesus Have a Wife and Children?
His laws do not change for his messengers either. The job of a messenger is to convey the Message. The results (reckoning) will be according to God’s rules that never change for anyone.

We did send Messengers before you, and appointed wives and children for them. It was not given to any Messenger that he could bring a sign  (the requital they hastened for) , but it came according to God’s Law of Respite [also 7:34]. For every rise and fall, there is a written law [Quran 13:38]

All Messengers were mortal human beings [3:144] and they conveyed God’s Revelation as commanded. Note that ‘all’ of them had wives and children and think of Jesus!

(O Messenger) whether We show you what We promise them, or cause you to die before that, your duty is to convey the Message. And the reckoning is Ours. [Quran 13:40]

title: The Quranic God
text:
Laws for Human Life (Psyche)
Just as invariant natural laws govern the physical universe — discovered through empirical observation and reason — an equally structured system of laws governs the non-physical realm: the human psyche, self, or soul (Nafs). These metaphysical principles dictate how individual actions imprint upon the inner self and ultimately shape the moral health and destiny of entire societies.
These spiritual and psychological laws are as fixed as gravity. Behavior driven by egoistic impulses and base desires pollutes the Nafs, leading to internal corruption and social fragmentation. Conversely, noble and selfless actions nourish the soul, fostering personal elevation and collective harmony. The Quran explicitly underscores this law of spiritual cause and effect:

And (regarding) the Nafs … Successful is he who nourishes/grows it. And failure is he who ruins/pollutes it. [Quran 91:7-10]

Just as certain physical laws involve deep complexity, the metaphysical principles governing the human psyche are intricately layered — amplified by the presence of human free will. Free will introduces a dynamic dimension of agency, allowing individual choices to alter the trajectory of lives and societies. Crucially, however, freedom of choice does not confer immunity from consequences; it grants autonomy over the action, while the outcome remains bound to immutable laws.
Consider a complex weather system as an analogy. Minute shifts in atmospheric variables can dramatically transform weather patterns. This sensitivity does not mean meteorology lacks underlying physical laws; rather, it reflects the vast number of interacting variables. In the same way, the moral and psychological laws governing human behavior and societal evolution remain consistent, even when the interplay of millions of individual choices makes exact outcomes difficult to predict.
Ultimately, while human beings possess the agency to choose, they exert no authority over the natural and spiritual laws that govern the results of those choices. A person may freely choose to pull a trigger, but no effort of will can undo the physical and moral reality of the bullet’s impact. Likewise, a leader possesses the freedom to speak, yet remains powerless to prevent the inevitable ripple effects of those words across the collective consciousness of a society. Agency belongs to the individual; consequences belong to the law.

title: The Quranic God
text:
The Role of Free Will
Free will is the cornerstone of moral accountability and human responsibility. Legal frameworks, ethical standards, and social contracts all rest upon the premise that humans possess authentic agency. Without the freedom to evaluate options and choose between them, concepts like virtue, justice, and moral responsibility become empty abstractions.
Certain contemporary neuroscientists point to pre-conscious neural activity preceding conscious awareness to argue that free will is an illusion. Yet this objection focuses primarily on instantaneous, reactionary behavior — split-second responses forged under stress or driven by deeply ingrained habits.
While quick reflexes may operate on a cognitive autopilot, this does not negate free agency. We remain fully responsible for the habits we cultivate over time and for deciding whether to reinforce or override those automatic patterns.
Crucially, human life is not merely a sequence of unreflective reflexes. We regularly encounter moments that afford space for quiet contemplation, allowing reason, values, and deliberate reflection to guide our choices. This capacity for conscious deliberation — stepping back from impulse to evaluate purpose — is precisely what elevates human conduct above mere animal instinct.
Though instant reactions may be automatic, we retain both the power and the obligation to curate our choices, actively sculpting the trajectory of our inner self (the Nafs).
Conclusion
In both the physical cosmos and the interior landscape of the human psyche, invariant divine laws govern every outcome. While human free will introduces dynamic complexity into the world, it never grants immunity from the underlying law of cause and effect. The immutable principles governing the Nafs affirm a timeless truth:
actions that cultivate virtue elevate the soul, while self-serving choices inflict spiritual decay. 
Ultimately, our choices are not lost to the void — they actively forge our inner character and ripple outward to shape the collective destiny of human society.

title: Atheism
text:
Science explores the observable universe, but it can’t reach beyond the Big Bang or our universe. Scientists can make hypotheses about multi-universes based on what they see here, but they have no way to prove or disprove them. Thus, science is a powerful tool for understanding our universe, but it does not have the capacity to confirm or deny the existence of God. Expecting science to prove one way or the other would tantamount to misunderstanding science.
Agnostics acknowledge this lack of scientific evidence and stay neutral on the question of God. Atheists, however, reject the existence of God, seeing no scientific reason to believe. Interestingly, logical reasoning can prove the existence of God, but only if one is open-minded.
It’s wise to distance oneself from any religion that promotes illogical dogmas, oppressive behavior, and allows atrocious acts against non-believers or followers of other faiths. However, the question of God’s existence is separate from the lies told in His name by some believers.
To find the truth, we must approach the subject rationally, examining all evidence without bias. Atheists, who pride themselves on rationality, should also rely on reason and critical thinking, avoiding speculative assumptions about a higher being.
In this discussion, we present logical arguments to prove the existence of a “Higher Being”. This term refers not to a deity bound by religious doctrine, but to an ultimate reality that exists independently and essentially, without relying on anything else. By making this distinction, we aim to foster a fair and thoughtful dialogue, free of misconceptions or prejudices.
We invite everyone to engage meaningfully with an open mind. Please, set aside societal influences and personal desires, and consider the arguments based on their merit.

title: Atheism
text:
Existence and Reality
Before we delve into the matter, it’s worth contemplating the notion of existence. What does it mean to exist? While most people accept their existence and the world around them as self-evident, this assumption is worth examining. Consider the possibility that everything you know is part of a dream — your dream. How would you distinguish this dream from reality?
Alternatively, imagine being connected to a machine that generates a simulated reality for your mind. Your sensory experiences are manipulated, and you cannot tell that this reality is artificial. Can such a machine make you doubt your own existence? Of course not!
The very act of doubting your existence is proof that you exist, because you cannot create a doubt in someone or something that does not exist. In addition, doubt requires a conscious, self-aware entity to experience it. Therefore, while a dream or a machine might deceive your senses, it cannot erase your fundamental self-awareness.
Though experiments like these can affirm our own existence, they leave us uncertain about the nature of the reality beyond ourselves. Whether our world is real or not, the arguments we are going to present remain valid. For simplicity, we will assume that the world we observe is “real.”
Within this context, we define two types of realities: conditioned and unconditioned.

Conditioned Reality
A reality that depends on external factors for its existence at any given moment. In other words, its existence is conditional upon certain conditions being met at the moment of its existence.
For instance, you as a human being rely on organs, air, and countless other conditions to exist. All these conditions need to be present for your existence. Take, for example, a cat, which depends on its cells, molecules, atoms, etc. and their specific organization or structure to maintain its existence. These dependencies extend to everything in the observable universe, including particles, waves, and even the laws of physics.


Unconditioned Reality
A reality that exists independently, requiring no external conditions to sustain it. This is often described as an “uncaused cause” or a foundational existence.

title: Atheism
text:
The Approach
Before proceeding to the actual arguments, it is worth recalling that proof by contradiction is a common and powerful method used in both mathematics and logic to demonstrate the validity of a statement. In the absence of observable evidence, proof by contradiction is a useful method of proving or disproving logical assertions. We intend to use this method to prove the existence of an Unconditioned Reality - the Higher Being.
Proof by contradiction works by assuming the opposite of what one wishes to prove. For example, to prove that a Higher Being exists, one assumes that a Higher Being does not exist. Then, logical arguments are presented showing that the assumption leads to a contradiction. If such a contradiction arises, it can be concluded that the assumption was wrong and not viable, thus proving the validity of the original assertion. This method works only when there are two possiblities that are disjoint - meaning one of them must be true but never both.
For an “Unconditioned Reality”, there are two mutually exclusive possibilities: either it exists or not. We will use the described method to prove its exists.

title: Atheism
text:
The Proof
We want to prove that an Unconditioned Reality exists, and at this time, we do not know if it exists or not. But one thing is certain: you exist, and you rely on many realities for your existence. Thus, it is obvious that some realities exist.
Now, for the sake of argument, let’s assume that an Unconditioned Reality does not exist.
This assumption implies that the world consists of only conditioned realities. The set of these realities can either be finite or infinite. Let’s consider both cases one by one.


A Finite Set of Conditioned Realities (case 1)
For simplicity, consider the case of your existence. You are a conditioned reality, dependent on cells and their specific organization. The cells are conditioned realities and depend on molecules and their structures. The molecules, in turn, are also conditioned realities as they rely on subsequent realities. Let’s assume the last in the chain of these dependencies is called ‘x’.
Being a conditioned reality, ‘x’ cannot exist because the reality it depends on does not exist—recall ‘x’ is the last one in the chain. If ‘x’ does not exist, the entire chain of dependencies falls apart like a domino effect. If none of the dependent realities exist, you cannot exist either. But that is a contradiction because you exist.
Thus, the assumption of the non-existence of Unconditioned Reality leads to a contradiction; therefore, the assumption was not valid.
The same argument can also be represented by the following figure, where conditioned reality-1 depends on conditioned reality-2, which in turn depends on conditioned reality-3, and so on until the last conditioned reality-x:
reality_1← reality_2← ... reality_x←
Since the reality that reality-x depends on does not exist, none of the realities in the chain exist. The same argument can be repeated for any number of conditioned realities. In the absence of an “Unconditioned Reality,” none can exist.


Finite Set with Circular Dependency (case 2)
One could argue that the contradiction problem can be avoided if the last conditioned reality-x depends on the first conditioned reality-1. This dependency chain is shown in the following figure, where reality-1 is shown twice only for the purpose of clarity - reality-x depending on reality-1:
reality_1← reality_2← ... reality_x← reality_1←
This arrangement creates a problem of self-dependence, where reality_1 depends on itself through the chain of intermediaries. This setup implies that conditioned reality_1 must sustain, through intermediaries, its own existence, which is a logical impossibility.
A reality cannot cause its own existence because it would need to exist prior to itself to fulfill the dependency. Therefore, this arrangement also leads to a contradiction.
Both of these cases have demonstrated that a set of finite conditioned realities cannot exist, unless the assumption is invalid.


An Infinite Set of Conditioned Realities
Next, consider the case of an infinite set of conditioned realities, which can be shown in the following dependency chain figure:
reality_1← reality_2← ... reality_x← ...
Let’s first consider an alternative arrangement, for simplicity, where an infinite number of conditioned realities exist between the first conditioned reality-1 and the last conditioned reality-x, as shown below within the parenthesis:
reality_1← (... reality_y← ...) reality_x←
This arrangement is no different from the case of finite conditioned realities with reality-x being the last. As long as the reality that reality-x depends on does not exist, none of the other realities exist, even if they are infinite.
Even if you rearrange these conditioned realities where there is no last conditioned reality and the chain is infinite, the fact remains that none of those can exist on their own because all are conditioned realities. But, we know that realities exist; hence, this case also leas to a contradiction.

It is to be noted that based on how a conditioned reality was defined in terms of “simultaneous existence of dependencies,” the infinite regress challenge is not valid for this case.
Simultaneous Existence of Dependencies
For a conditioned reality to exist, all the conditions it depends on must exist simultaneously. For example, a cat cannot exist unless its cells, molecules, and atoms exist at the same time. This requirement holds for every link in the chain.
Infinite Regress
Infinite regress refers to a scenario where a chain of dependencies extends indefinitely without ever reaching a foundational cause. Imagine an infinite chain of causes and effects, where each effect depends on a prior cause. In such a scenario, the process of cause-and-effect would require infinite time to reach any particular point, making the existence of the present moment impossible.
In the current scenario, all dependent realities must exist now simultaneously for a conditioned reality to exist, even if they are infinite. This is impossible because none of them can exist on their own and rely on some other reality for their existence.

From the above cases, it becomes evident that conditioned realities cannot exist on their own, whether arranged in a finite or infinite set.
The contradictions in both scenarios demonstrate that our assumption - “no unconditioned reality exists” - is false. Therefore, the existence of an unconditioned reality is necessary to sustain all conditioned realities.
An unconditioned reality, by definition, exists independently and does not rely on any external factors. It serves as the ultimate foundation, providing the necessary support for all dependent realities.


Conclusion
We began with the assumption that no unconditioned reality exists and explored all possible configurations of conditioned realities. Each scenario led to contradictions, proving the assumption untenable. Thus, we conclude that an unconditioned reality must exist.

title: Atheism
text:
A Word of Caution
This unconditioned reality is not bound by the limitations of conditioned realities and serves as the foundational cause of all existence. While this proof establishes its existence, it does not imply the characteristics or nature of this reality beyond its independence and necessity. As such, any claims about its attributes should be critically evaluated based on further evidence and rational inquiry.

title: Atheism
text:
The Uncaused, Indivisible, and One
Here, we will present the proof for the oneness of unconditioned reality.
The concept of an unconditioned reality must be “indivisible”. If it were comprised of parts or subcomponents, it would not be an unconditioned reality (consider the relationship between a cat and its components). As such, the idea of a higher being cannot be divided into two or more entities in one. By definition, this higher being must also be uncaused (not depending on any condition or cause.)
If there were “multiple” unconditioned realities, they would either be identical or differ in some aspect. If they differed, there would be some aspect of differences between them. However, this would suggest that the realities have parts (with differing and similar aspects), making them dependent on those components, which leads to absurdity (as they are unconditioned realities.) Therefore, the existence of multiple unconditioned realities is an impossibility.
The possibility of multiple “identical” realities is also eliminated. According to the principle of the Identity of Indiscernible by Leibniz, if there are multiple realities, they must be identical.
It is incorrect to consider identical realities as occupying separate areas in space, as space is part of the conditioned realities, which cannot exist independently. The idea of multiple identical unconditioned realities is therefore invalid.
Therefore, there is only One, Indivisible, Uncaused reality, commonly referred to as God or a Higher Being.

title: Objections
text:
If a proof for the existence of an Uncaused Cause exists, atheists lack a valid basis to deny the existence of God. While one might reject specific religious interpretations of how God operates in our lives or in the world, the existence of God itself cannot be reasonably dismissed. Let’s examine some of the common objections and questions raised by atheists.
The claim that “God cannot be scientifically proven” is not a sound argument but rather a reflection of the limitations inherent in our scientific methods. The absence of scientific evidence should not be mistaken for evidence against God’s existence. Science, by its nature, operates within a framework of assumptions and principles that themselves cannot be proven.
The existence of God has been demonstrated through logical and mathematical reasoning in Part 1, not mere blind faith. Recognizing the limits of scientific methods invites us to consider proofs and arguments beyond empirical evidence.
This statement misrepresents the essence of scientific understanding. Historically, even great minds like Aristotle suggested that life could arise spontaneously, a belief held by scientists for over two millennia. Similarly, contemporary statements about quantum physics are often misunderstood or oversimplified.
Quantum physics operates on the concept of the quantum field, which undergoes spontaneous fluctuations. However, the root cause of these fluctuations remains unknown. The lack of current understanding does not equate to the absence of an underlying cause. To assert otherwise is to mistake a gap in knowledge for proof of randomness or “nothingness.”
While Stephen Hawking proposed that the laws of physics could lead to the spontaneous creation of the universe, this idea requires closer scrutiny. Laws, by definition, describe how entities behave — they do not possess causal power. For instance, the law of gravity describes the attraction between masses but does not cause or generate that attraction.
This perspective also raises deeper questions: What ensures that matter consistently behaves according to these laws? What or who establishes these laws in the first place? Without addressing such fundamental issues, the claim remains incomplete and speculative.
The assertion that “the universe is eternal and infinite” is an unproven assumption. The corresponding claim that “there is no need for God” is not a scientific conclusion but a subjective perspective. Statements beginning with “if” inherently reflect hypothetical scenarios unless substantiated by evidence.
Additionally, the argument overlooks key principles, such as the second law of thermodynamics. This law illustrates that systems naturally progress towards states of higher entropy or disorder. For example, when a cup breaks, the probability of it spontaneously reassembling into its original form is nearly zero. Extending this concept, it is even more improbable for a universe of such immense complexity and harmony to arise spontaneously or exist eternally in its current state.
Despite its remarkable advancements, science remains unable to answer certain fundamental questions:
Natural laws merely describe observed behaviors; they do not explain the underlying causes of those behaviors.
By carefully reviewing the proof provided in Part 1, it becomes evident that the idea of an eternal or infinite existence of conditioned realities (like matter) is logically untenable. These conditioned realities must rely on an Uncaused Cause, usually termed as Yehweh, God, or Allah.
Contrary to this claim, proof of the One, Indivisible, Uncaused Reality has been provided in Part 1. Belief in the “non-existence” of God or the eternity of matter, however, remains a matter of blind faith. Atheists, who often emphasize rationality, offer no concrete proof for their assertions. Their arguments frequently rely on subjective reasoning or wishful thinking rather than logical and evidence-based conclusions.
The question of suffering is less a challenge to God’s existence and more an exploration of observed reality. Without a Divine Being, concepts like suffering, morality, and justice lose their objective meaning. For instance, no scientific law can label the atrocities of the Nazi concentration camps as “wrong.” Science operates in the realm of observable phenomena and measurable facts; it does not address emotions, values, or ethics.
A Divine framework is necessary to anchor these concepts. Without it, terms like “right” and “wrong” become arbitrary, defined only by human preference or societal norms.

title: Objections
text:
Clarification: Cause-and-Effect and God’s Will
The concepts of natural laws and God’s will are not mutually exclusive; rather, they coexist harmoniously. God, through His free will, upholds the natural laws that govern the universe, ensuring their consistency and reliability. While humans are endowed with free will, they remain subject to these immutable laws. For example, a person can choose to place their hand in fire, but they cannot escape the law of burning that governs the fire’s behavior.
If God were to constantly alter the behavior of elements like fire, He might be seen as inconsistent or unpredictable. A flawless creation plan does not require adjustments. Consider the analogy of computer applications: human developers must release updates to address unforeseen issues, a reflection of our limited knowledge. By contrast, God’s omniscience ensures that His plan is perfect from the start, requiring no modifications. The fixed and unchanging nature of natural laws reflects this perfection.
This consistency in natural law also underscores God’s impartiality. Natural laws apply universally, without favoritism. Fire burns both believers and non-believers alike, and gravity affects everyone equally. This universal fairness is a hallmark of God’s Kingdom, demonstrating that His justice extends to all, irrespective of their beliefs.

title: Rational thinking
text:
Humans have the capability to think and reason. When we think rationally, we analyze past experiences, explore possibilities, evaluate evidence, and make facts-driven conclusions. But how often do we pull the entire process through? A lot of the time, we shortcut the process and call fast-thinking rational-thinking.
Consider swimming for example. You learn swimming in shallow waters before jumping into deep waters. Second, you cannot shortcut the swimming process. There are four phases in a freestyle swimming stroke: 1) catch, 2) pull, 3) exit, and 4) recovery. You swim only by completing all four phases. Third, you cannot swim half-way to the middle of the river and assume you are done for the day.

title: Rational thinking
text:
Learning never ends
When children do not understand anything, they observe others and ask questions. Asking right questions is the first step towards understanding anything and adults teach children to formulate the questions before answering. As we grow older, we pose questions (to ourselves), find answers, and update our understanding.
For example, we update our beliefs in the light of new facts and evidence. No one now believes that magic, spirit, devil, or an angel carries the sound of a person from one part of the planet to the other when talking over a phone.

Learning does not stop at any level … It is a life-long journey.

title: Rational thinking
section: Solving the hard questions, the wrong way
text:
Solving the hard questions, the wrong way
Some questions are hard to answer. We replace them with questions that are quicker to answer. For example, if you win or lose in a match, you may replace the question, ‘What were the reasons you won or lost?’ with ‘Is God kind or unkind to you?’ Such fast-thinking hacks, in many cases, make our reasoning unsound and our understanding of the world inconsistent.
For example, we may develop a faith-based understanding of the world that is inconsistent with reality. This happens when we are unwilling to let go of false beliefs or frivolous ideas that are dear to us. The differences between the two generate conflicting models of the future in our predictive brain. We rush to resolve the uneasiness and fear generated by ambivalence in the future (outcome).
Since we cannot change the physical laws, nor do we want to let our faith go, we box our beliefs in a separate mental chambers. We do not let any fact or evidence infiltrate these chambers that can invalidate our beliefs.


Our brain does not like inconsistent views of the world based on faith versus facts. To resolve the conflict, we compartmentalize our brain. We restrict, re-interpret, or even twist the evidence in mental chambers that guard our faith.

title: Rational thinking
section: Thinking is neither cheap nor easy
text:
Thinking is neither cheap nor easy
Thinking is an exhaustive activity that consumes energy. The process of thinking demands your focus and time. Fact-finding activities, necessary for making an informed decision, require money and resources. As some of the resources are limited and hard to acquire, the job of rational thinking becomes riddled with hurdles.
Hurdles pave the way for a fast-thinking brain. Fast thinking brain does not waste time on deep analysis. Instead, it jumps to a conclusion in minimal time to save energy and resources. It does so based on partial data, quickly available from recent experiences, repeated memories, our likenesses and dislikes, etc.
If a decision leads to immediate gains, a strong feedback loop becomes an incentive for further fast thinking. Losses may also give you an incentive for fast thinking to save whatever you can: time, energy and resources used on rational thinking that can potentially lead to the same outcome.
Ultimately, our brain goes fully into an autopilot mode, where fast-thinking takes the driving seat of our reasoning. For example, we follow rituals because it is the most convenient thing to do that requires no thinking at all. A fast-thinking brain does not have the capacity or courage to challenge the sanity of an entire group, including our loved ones who follow the same rituals. The probability of them all going wrong is extremely low if not zero.


“How can they all be so irrational when it comes to faith while they are reasonable in other worldly affairs? In addition, if the rituals have been in practice for so many centuries, previous generations must have already vetted those beliefs, right?”


Once an action has already been taken, it is not worth looking at reasons that could make us look irrational. We ignore the facts that prove us wrong and search for information that supports our actions. Over time, the accumulated (but partial) knowledge in our favor makes our faith stronger.
Some politicians and regimes take advantage of this human weakness. They make false claims and then keep rehashing time and again. When repeated enough times, people start believing in the plausibility of the claim. Instead of asking for proof of the claim, rejectors of the false claim are asked to prove their case.

Fast thinking optimizes energy, time, and resources. Once you believe in a false claim, your brain creates a separate mental box for the claims made by the person you just believed in. You accept all those claims to be (at least somewhat) true and pass the burden of proof on to the ones who deny the claims.

In addition, humans are social animals who assign very high value to activities that generate a sense of belonging. We feel a sense of belonging to a group when we follow the unique social and religious activities that define the group. Without group identity, we feel lonely and abandoned.
Where does the fear of abandonment come from? In ancient times, a lonely and fragile human was no match for wild animals or hostile groups. Sense of belonging kept humans together and alive.
We may have killed all the wild animals and created punishment laws for hurting other humans, but the desire for belonging still lingers on strongly deep within us. Belonging to a group is not a bad idea, but we sacrifice our own identity and behave like a herd.

title: Rational thinking
text:
Conclusion
Rationality is not about finding justification for our beliefs and actions. Rather, it is about finding truth. Desires should be kept aside, and unbiased evidence should be analyzed as objectively as humanly possible. Assumption should not be made a priori, and facts should not be ignored based on our liking or disliking. We must be ready, in all honesty, to accept the reason-based decision even if we do not like it.
The good news is that we can change at any time no matter how hard our habits might have become. Just like we have trained ourselves to act on fast thinking, we can gradually train ourselves to engage in rational thinking. The more you use your reasoning faculties, the more efficient you become at using it.

title: Inherited religion
text:
Where you are born largely dictates what you believe. Before a child ever learns to reason, their worldview is already shaped by the geography, culture, and faith of their parents.
Across the globe, human convictions form a vast and complex mosaic:
If you are Muslim, non-Muslims outnumber you nearly three to one. Christians face a similar numerical reality. Yet truth is not a democracy; popularity offers zero guarantee of validity, and sheer numbers do not convert inherited assumptions into objective reality.
Intellectual clarity and moral discernment are not tied to ethnic origin, religious ancestry, or geographical luck. History shows that groundbreaking contributions to science, philosophy, and human understanding have emerged from every corner of the earth—just as human beings across all traditions regularly succumb to unexamined, irrational habits.

title: Inherited religion
text:
The mechanics of inherited orthodoxy
The vast majority of people do not choose their core beliefs through objective inquiry; they inherit them as cultural default settings. Consider the typical experience within Christian communities—though the dynamic applies universally: children are immersed in religious rituals, attend church, listen to clerical authorities, and absorb foundational dogmas long before their critical faculties have developed. Over time, external conditioning hardens into internal identity.
When an individual begins to question these inherited constructs, their community often responds with suspicion, labeling them a heretic, dissenter, or outsider.
This epistemic inertia is hardly confined to religion. Millions hold unexamined secular, political, or economic ideologies with religious fervor. In both realms, genuine critical thinking is routinely sacrificed on the altar of tradition.

title: Inherited religion
text:
Convenience, desire, and selective skepticism
When people break away from inherited traditions, the shift is rarely driven by pure logic alone. Personal desires and psychological convenience often steer the outcome.
An atheist, for example, might reject institutional religion after recognizing its internal contradictions, yet stop short of investigating broader metaphysical possibilities. Stepping away from religious oversight can offer an appealing sense of personal autonomy, but if driven purely by convenience, it risks dismissing profound truths along with cultural baggage.
Belief systems—whether religious, secular, or dogmatically atheist—frequently serve self-interested ends. Science may debunk primitive superstitions, but it cannot rule out the existence of a foundational Creator. Rejecting the concept of a Higher Being simply because it imposes unwanted boundaries is not an exercise in rationality; it is emotional preference disguised as intellectual liberation.

Herd mentality: The security of tribal consensus
Human beings are wired for social cohesion. The desire for belonging often overrides the pursuit of truth, leading to herd mentality: the uncritical adoption of surrounding beliefs to maintain harmony with the group.
Consider the internal struggle of Michael, a devout believer grappling with dogmas that conflict with his basic logic:
Michael’s Internal Conflict:

“How could my parents, my pastors, and generations of brilliant scholars all be wrong? Surely someone along the line has thoroughly investigated and validated these foundational truths… right?”

Diana’s Resignation: His younger sister, Diana, confronts the same dissonance but chooses intellectual surrender:

“If the doctrine doesn’t make sense to me, the flaw must lie in my own intellect. How could millions of believers across centuries possibly be mistaken?”

The Parental Justification: Their parents complete the cycle of consensus bias:

“How could a belief system sustained by millions of people over thousands of years be founded on an illusion? Such widespread consensus across generations cannot be a mistake!”

This self-reinforcing loop—where each generation defers to the authority of the previous one without independent verification—is the hallmark of herd mentality.
Breaking free demands immense intellectual courage. Yet the reward is true independence: a mind capable of evaluating reality without reliance on cultural crutches.
Note: While this scenario features a Christian family, the psychological dynamic is identical across Islamic, Hindu, Jewish, secular, or ideological environments.
The Trap of Scholastic Deference
Even revered scholars and theologians frequently fall into this trap. Rather than testing foundational axioms against reason and evidence, they often defer to the consensus of past authorities, assuming historical precedent is infallible. When logic reaches a dead end, they default to the assertion that faith requires an uncritical leap beyond reason.
The blind followers argue:


… Indeed, we found our (pious) fathers upon a religion and indeed we are in their footsteps (rightly) guided! [Quran 43:22]




… they say, “Good enough for us is that upon which we found our fathers..” [Quran 5:104]


While God counters:


… “(such blind followers are) deaf, dumb, and blind, so they do not use their intellect.” [Quran 2:171]

title: Inherited religion
text:
Conclusion
Herd mentality is a subtle form of intellectual captivity. It encourages passive acceptance and penalizes genuine inquiry. To break free, one must cultivate the courage to question ancestral defaults, dismantle unexamined assumptions, and demand objective evidence. Truth is not an inheritance to be passively received; it is a pursuit that demands personal accountability, active reasoning, and unwavering intellectual integrity.

title: Intellectual blindness
text:
Navigating life’s complexities is daunting enough, but discovering a universal blueprint for human guidance is an extraordinary feat. The far greater challenge, however, is communicating that solution to a vast and diverse world. A rigid, one-size-fits-all approach inevitably fails when faced with the infinite spectrum of human language, culture, and intellect. To truly resonate—whether speaking to a villager in a remote corner of the globe or a seasoned academic in the halls of higher learning—the message must adapt to the recipient’s context and level of understanding.
If the purpose of the Quran was to serve as a timeless guide for all humanity, it must transcend the cultural and historical constraints of seventh-century Arabia. Its style must remain as vibrant and profound today as it was when first revealed. Such a text cannot rely on static formulas; it must deliver enduring principles that continually invite fresh reflection across every era.
To bridge this gap, the Quran uses a dynamic, captivating discourse capable of engaging the human soul while exploring deep psychological and philosophical truths. Rather than offering dry, technical treatises on ethics and behavior, it weaves allegories, symbols, and vivid metaphors into narratives rich with layered meaning.
Consider how effectively creative narrative conveys abstract ideas. In H.G. Wells’ The Country of the Blind, physical sightlessness becomes an evocative allegory for human closed-mindedness and epistemic inertia. In the same way, the Quran employs storytelling and profound metaphors to translate complex realities into accessible, thought-provoking lessons that speak directly to both the intellect and the heart.

title: Intellectual blindness
text:
Metaphors in the Quran
Metaphors in the Quran serve as timeless communicative bridges, weaving vivid imagery that transcends linguistic, cultural, and chronological boundaries. Rather than reducing guidance to rigid legalisms or dry abstraction, these visual allegories speak directly to human intuition across ages.
One central metaphor is blindness — a state of cognitive surrender where individuals abandon logic and critical reasoning, allowing unexamined emotions, biases, and inherited desires to dictate their worldview. This intellectual myopia fosters an uncritical acceptance of baseless dogmas, shuttering the mind against empirical reality and the pursuit of objective truth.
Similarly, the Quran invokes death as an allegory for intellectual stagnation and moral decay, applicable to both individuals and entire civilizations. It portrays a state of living inertia: a condition where a person remains physically active yet entirely unresponsive to truth, evidence, or constructive dialogue — akin to addressing a corpse. This stark image highlights the urgent necessity of intellectual awakening, calling for a transition from passive existence to a vibrant, reflective, and purposeful life.
By bypassing dense academic jargon in favor of such evocative metaphors, the Quran communicates multi-layered truths with enduring clarity. This approach engages both analytical reason and existential awareness, ensuring its core message remains universally compelling regardless of a reader’s background or era.

[Intellectually] Blind and the seeing are not equal. Nor are the darknesses and the light … And the living and the dead are not alike … [Quran 35:19-22]

Here, the Quran eloquently casts itself as the light — a luminous guide navigating humanity through intellectual and moral confusion. In contrast, unexamined dogmas and irrational assumptions are portrayed as darkness. The capacity for critical inquiry and objective reasoning is celebrated as “seeing,” while obstinate adherence to baseless beliefs is condemned as “blindness.” These vivid allegories underscore a fundamental premise: true spiritual awakening cannot occur without rigorous intellectual engagement.
Much like navigating pitch darkness requires both a lantern and functioning sight, meaningful guidance demands two inseparable elements: the Quran as the objective source of truth (the light) and active human intellect (the seeing eyes) to perceive and comprehend it.

Just as the brightest light offers no utility to a closed eye, the Quran’s profound guidance cannot be realized without a discerning, courageous, and reflective mind.

title: Intellectual blindness
text:
The Blindness
A core theme throughout the Quran is the liberating mission of God’s messengers: to free humanity from the shackles of inherited dogma and collective conformity. Rather than demanding uncritical submission, these messengers aimed to awaken the individual’s dormant capacity for reason, empowering people to evaluate truth through evidence, logic, and self-reflection.
Yet time and again, this call to intellectual freedom met fierce resistance. Entrenched in tribal pride and psychological comfort, communities defaulted to ancestral loyalty: “We will not abandon the path of our forefathers, regardless of logic or evidence.” This reflexive rejection illustrates the immense grip of inherited tradition, which frequently overrides clear reason and empirical reality.
Take the narrative of Prophet Noah, who challenged his community to abandon the hollow practice of idol worship. Rather than testing their assumptions or engaging in honest inquiry, they retreated behind ancestral precedent, dismissing rational critique simply because it diverged from the ways of their elders.

(They said,) ‘… We never heard such (a rational evaluation of faith) from our elders (and sages) of earlier generations.’ [Quran 23:23-24]

This psychological resistance—where loyalty to ancestral precedent eclipses rational evaluation—is hardly an isolated relic of the past; it is a universal human vulnerability that spans cultures, eras, and ideologies. The Quran underscores the persistence of this flaw by documenting a recurring pattern across history: whenever a prophet called people to reason, the dominant culture defended its cognitive inertia under the banner of tradition.
Consider Prophet Saleh, who urged his community to abandon the worship of lifeless, hollow deities. Their response epitomized the psychological barrier of inherited authority over critical inquiry:

They said, ‘O Saleh! We had placed great hopes in you before this! But how dare you tell us to move away from worshiping what our elders worshiped? …’ [Quran 11:62]

A parallel dynamic unfolds with Prophet Abraham, who directly challenged his father and community regarding their devotion to inanimate statues. Stripped of logical justification, their defense laid bare an underlying intellectual complacency:

When he (Abraham) said to his father and his people, ‘What are these images and statues to which you are devoted (Give me some rational reasoning for your behavior)?’ They responded, ‘We found our elders worshiping them’ (Beliefs require blind following and not critical thinking.) [Quran 21:52-53]

This reflexive appeal to the past persisted even in the presence of undeniable evidence. When Prophet Moses confronted Pharaoh and his court with compelling arguments, they systematically evaded the rational challenge, retreating into ancestral precedent:

They said, ‘Have you come to divert us (with your reasoning skills) from what we found our elders practicing? …’ [Quran 10:78]

This exact pattern repeated during the era of Prophet Muhammad. Confronted with clear arguments, defenders of the status quo dismissed rational inquiry altogether, framing the call to critical thought as a subversive attempt to undermine their cultural heritage:

When Our Ayaat (signs) are conveyed to them in all clarity, they say, ‘This is only a man who wants to divert you from what your elders used to worship.’ and they (further) say, ‘This is nothing but an invented lie.’ … [Quran 34:43]

When invited to evaluate the rational guidance of the Quran, they again retreated into uncritical tribal allegiance:

When it is said to them, ‘Follow what (rational guidance) God has revealed (in the Quran)’, they say, ‘Nay! We will follow the ways of our elders.’ What! Even though their elders were lacking in understanding and were not rightly guided? [Quran 2:170]


Rather, they say, “Indeed, we found our elders upon a religion, and we are in their footsteps [rightly] guided.” [Quran 43:22]


… they say, ‘Enough for us is what we found our elders doing.’ What! Even though their elders had no knowledge whatsoever and no guidance?’ [Quran 5:104]


These Quranic historical narratives vividly demonstrate the enduring challenge of overcoming cognitive blindness and breaking free from the momentum of ancestral tradition. They stand as a timeless reminder that authentic truth cannot be inherited; it must be individually sought, tested, and verified through critical reasoning.

title: Intellectual blindness
text:
Herd Mentality
The Quran places individual accountability and cognitive autonomy at the very heart of spiritual maturity. It sharply critiques those who abdicate their reasoning to religious authorities or social pressure, comparing “blind followers” to livestock that follow a shepherd’s call without understanding its meaning. This uncritical obedience is not a virtue; it is a failure to exercise the distinctively human capacity for thought.

The likeness of truth-rejecters (due to blind following) is that (of a sheep) which hears the shepherd’s call but hears in it nothing more than a sound and a shout (to be followed blindly). [Intellectually] Deaf, dumb, blind, for they do not use their reason [عقل]. [Quran 2:171]

In another vivid allegory, the Quran depicts those who anchor their identity exclusively in ancestral precedent as people attempting to navigate forward while “staring perpetually backward.” By fixating on the past, they remain oblivious to the realities and evidence directly before them.

On the Day when their faces shall be tossed about in the fire (looking backward), they will say, ‘Oh, We wish we had obeyed God, and obeyed the Messenger!’ (who asked us to ponder over what was right in front of us.) .. And they will (further) say, ‘Our Lord! We obeyed our revered clergy and the leaders and it is those who led us astray from the path .. Our Lord! Give them double punishment and banish them from Your grace.’ [Quran 33:66-68]

This stark imagery serves as an urgent warning: outsourcing one’s intellect to institutional (religious) leaders or societal consensus offers no protection when confronted with ultimate reality. The Quran demands a forward-looking, intellectually active engagement with truth — one rooted in personal reflection rather than the comfort of the herd.

title: Intellectual blindness
text:
Religious Leaders and Their Followers
Religious leaders and scholars who exploit their authority to promote dogmatic error bear a double burden of responsibility. They carry the consequences of their own cognitive blindness alongside the gravity of steering whole communities away from rational inquiry.

They shall bear their burdens undiminished on Resurrection Day, with part of the burdens of those whom they misled … Ah, evil is what they bear! [Quran 16:25]

Yet followers cannot escape their own individual accountability. Submitting blindly to clerical authority does not absolve anyone of the fundamental duty to exercise their own reason and judgment. In the end, passive conformity offers no defense. The Quran depicts these uncritical followers in the depths of ruins — a state of intense internal turmoil and societal breakdown — engaged in bitter, futile arguments with the very leaders they uncritically obeyed, consumed by regret for abdicating their own intellect.

… If you could only see these transgressors when they are made to stand before their Lord, how they blame one another. The followers will tell their proud leaders, ‘If it were not for you, we would have been believers.’ [Quran 34:31]

The Quran draws a striking parallel between those who abandon their analytical faculties and animals that must be externally controlled. Just as physical restraints are placed on creatures driven purely by instinct, those who forfeit their capacity for reason subject themselves to the ultimate form of captivity—intellectual and spiritual bondage.

… Both parties (religious leaders and their blind followers) will be filled with remorse when they see the doom. We will put shackles around the necks of all those who rejected the truth. Should they be rewarded with anything else except for what they used to do (i.e., behaving like animals)? [Quran 34:33]

By refusing to engage the mind, an individual forfeits the very quality that defines human dignity, reducing their existence to mere reactive impulse. This imagery delivers a profound philosophical warning: intellectual accountability cannot be delegated. Every human being, regardless of status or lineage, bears the personal responsibility to seek truth through active discernment. To outsource one’s intellect to external authorities or cultural momentum is to invite self-inflicted blindness, trading cognitive freedom for the perils of passive conformity.

title: Country of the blind
text:
Long ago, a hiker lost his footing along a treacherous ridge and tumbled down a steep mountainside, awakening in a hidden valley completely severed from the outside world. Centuries earlier, a cataclysmic earthquake had sealed off this secluded haven with massive walls of rock. Though the outside world assumed its inhabitants had long since perished, the community had actually survived—and over generations, quietly flourished in complete isolation.
Not long after the catastrophe, a genetic ocular disease began spreading through the isolated population, ultimately rendering each new generation blind from birth. Confronted with an uncertain future, the community’s elders crafted ingenious adaptations, refining their routines to navigate a world devoid of visual light. As centuries rolled by, the lived memory of sight evaporated into legend, until blindness was no longer recognized as a loss, but embraced as the natural, universal order of human existence.
When the hiker regained consciousness and surveyed his new surroundings, he realized he had fallen into what could only be described as a “Country of the Blind.” Viewing himself as the proverbial “one-eyed king,” he attempted to explain the world as perceived through visual sight, describing the radiant warmth of the sun, the glittering beauty of the stars, and the precise physical origin of birdsong. Yet his words fell on deaf ears; to a society built entirely around touch, sound, and scent, these visual descriptions were incomprehensible and meaningless.
To the valley’s inhabitants, the hiker was not an enlightened guide, but a deeply flawed anomaly. Having honed their non-visual senses to extraordinary levels, they perceived his awkward movement in the dark as severe clumsiness and his insistence on an invisible phenomenon as a unsettling deficiency. His attempts to articulate a broader reality clashed directly with their deeply ingrained beliefs, destabilizing the fragile consensus of their visionless world.
Over time, collective patience wore thin, and the hiker’s persistent challenges to their shared worldview alienated him further. Denounced as a heretic, he was initially ordered to leave; yet with the valley permanently blocked, the elders permitted him to remain only on the strict condition that he permanently renounce all talk of sight. Reluctantly, he acquiesced.
However, after falling in love with a young woman in the village, he felt an irresistible urge to reveal to her the transformative beauty of visual perception. Distressed by his strange claims, she reported him to the elders, who summoned the village doctor. After evaluating the outsider, the doctor arrived at a chilling diagnostic conclusion: the man’s “sight” was a psychological pathology—a diseased sensory illusion causing severe mental anguish and irrational delusions.
The physician proposed a radical therapeutic cure: surgical removal of the man’s eyes. Stripping him of his visual organs, the elders reasoned, would liberate him from his painful hallucinations, restore his mental clarity, and integrate him fully into the peaceful conformity of their society. Faced with this harrowing ultimatum, the hiker was forced to confront a profound existential choice—submit to surgical blindness for the sake of social acceptance, or cling to his vision and risk everything to remain whole.

The metaphors of sight and blindness
In H. G. Wells’ classic narrative The Country of the Blind, physical sightlessness serves as an incisive metaphor for systemic closed-mindedness and epistemic insularity. The secluded valley operates as a powerful allegory for dogmatic societies and insular echo chambers that elevate inherited traditions to absolute truths, branding critical inquiry as heresy and treating new perspectives as dangerous pathologies.
In philosophical and literary traditions, blindness frequently symbolizes intellectual stagnation—the refusal to exercise one’s cognitive and analytical faculties. Conversely, metaphorical “death” represents a state of complete moral apathy and cognitive indifference, where individuals become entirely immune to truth, evidence, and constructive dialogue. It embodies the passive, dismissive posture of intellectual surrender and the active rejection of personal growth.
This timeless allegory challenges us to examine the pervasive tension between tradition and critical reflection, the hidden cost of social conformity, and the profound courage required to seek, acknowledge, and defend a broader truth.

title: A critique of intellect
section: “Islamic Empire” and the Renaissance of Europe
text:
“Islamic Empire” and the Renaissance of Europe
The initial policies of the Islamic empire were supportive of reason-based thinking. Therefore, scientific learning and scholarship flourished throughout the empire. The conducive environment produced thousands of polymaths (scientists and scholars) during the first few hundred years.
A small list of Muslim mathematicians, astronomers, biologists, chemists, psychologists, economists, geographers, and philosophers, who were at the top of their fields in the entire world of their time, can be found on the Internet.
Al-gebra and al-gorithm are two of the most common phrases in mathematical and computer sciences, which bear the name of Muslim scientists born a thousand years ago — Geber (Jabir Bin Hayyan جابر بن حیّان ) died in 816 A.D. and Algorithmi (Al-Khwarizmi الخوارزمی ) died in 850 A.D., respectively. Whenever you see ‘al’ at the beginning of a scientific or scholarly term, chances are that it is a twisted form of an Arabic word. Hazen (Ibn al-Haytham ابن الہیثم ), Alberonius (Al-Bairuni البیرونی ) and Avicenna (Ibn-Sina ابن سینا ) were among the intellectuals whose works have survived to date, to some degree.
Although most of the original work from that era has been lost to history, it served as a steppingstone for the European Renaissance scholars and scientists. To build the scientific foundation, Europe was already translating and studying the writings of Muslim scholars by the end of the 11th century.

title: A critique of intellect
text:
Muhammad Iqbal’s Poetry
While Muslim intellectuals were the giants for the pre-Renaissance European scholars, Muslims themselves were gradually doing away with intellectual endeavors. title: So what!
text:
Given that the universe operates according to fixed natural laws, one might question whether belief in God holds any real significance. However, if we accept the existence of a Creator, as previously established, it follows that what happens next is not for us to decide but rests entirely with this Creator.
If the Creator had the power to bring us into existence, it is reasonable to conclude that He could recreate us at any time. Interestingly, advancements in genetics and technology suggest that humans may one day achieve feats like transferring their minds into younger replicas derived from their genetic code. If such possibilities exist within human imagination and ingenuity, how much more plausible is it that the original Creator could gather all the necessary components — both material and immaterial — to recreate us entirely?

Freedom, Responsibility, and the Afterlife
God does not interfere in human affairs, as humans have been granted the freedom of choice. However, this freedom comes with the responsibility to build a society rooted in compassion and mutual care. A selfless life paves the way for a harmonious existence — a paradise — while selfish desires create a hellish existence for those consumed by greed.
The paradise- and hell-like societies we experience are the collective outcomes of our actions in this life. Similarly, individual fates await us in the afterlife, determined by the choices we make during our lifetime. The paths we choose shape our ultimate destination, whether it be a paradise or a hell-like existence.
This discussion does not revolve around “irrational beliefs” or “meaningless rituals.” Instead, it underscores a practical and grounded approach to life — one that enhances our collective well-being on Earth and prepares us for the second stage of existence.

title: An unpredictable world
text:
The question of ultimate origins is as vast as the cosmos itself. To grasp how humanity came to be, one would need a temporal viewport—a machine capable of peeling back the layers of cosmic history to the moment before time itself began. In my imagination, I stepped inside such a vessel.
The device transported me to a realm I call the “Pewniverse”—a conceptual cosmos existing prior to our Big Bang. At first glance, this world was eerily familiar: a burning sun hung in the sky, a silver moon drifted through the night, and continents sat beneath vast oceans. But as I observed more closely, a deep and unsettling chaos revealed itself.
The sun did not rise reliably in the east; one morning it burst forth from the west, and the next it crested in the north. Rivers coiling through valleys did not merely flow toward the sea—on whim, their waters reversed course, climbing mountain peaks or drifting sideways into the air. The immutable principles of physics we take for granted were non-existent. In the Pewniverse, the fabric of reality was governed not by fixed laws, but by perpetual randomness.
On one afternoon, I encountered a man named Pewton sitting quietly beneath an apple tree. But no apple fell neatly upon his head. As a stem snapped, one apple shot upward into the clouds, another hovered motionless in mid-air, and a third exploded sideways. Pewton sat in absolute despair, unable to formulate a single equation or discover the law of gravity. In a cosmos devoid of consistency, science was impossible. Without predictable laws, there could be no wheels, no engines, no flight, and no civilization—only perpetual paralysis.

title: An unpredictable world
text:
Unpredictable God
One morning, as the sun flared unexpectedly out of the western horizon, a messenger descended with a divine proclamation:

“I am your Lord, the Creator of all that exists.”
“I am the Almighty, and I act purely on divine impulse. I possess the power to command the sun from any horizon, to force rivers up mountain peaks, to launch apples into the sky, and to bring forth children from virgins.”
“Look around you! I twist and shatter the natural order whenever I Will to demonstrate My miracles and My supreme Power. I am a Living God—not a passive watchmaker. Will you not surrender to My absolute control and find peace by abandoning your futile search for fixed laws?”

title: An unpredictable world
text:
Unpredictable Nonbelievers
The capricious Will of the Almighty was the obvious driving force behind every event in the Pewniverse, yet virtually no one believed the messenger. And why should they?
Where there is no pattern, there can be no recognition of design. To the inhabitants, reality felt like a chaotic arena where multiple feuding deities battled for control: one god demanding the sun rise in the east, another forcing it to the west; one pushing waters downhill, another hauling them upward. There was no single, coherent hand maintaining order.
Or perhaps, they reasoned, a single Creator, if He was really One, had fallen into a deep cosmic slumber, leaving the universe to wobble on its axis.
Or worse still: perhaps the Creator was awake, but plagued by an existential identity crisis—suffering from divine mood swings that required constant, theatrical displays of rule-breaking just to reassure Himself of His own power.

title: An unpredictable world
text:
Our Sweet Predictable World
By contrast, we are privileged to inhabit a cosmos of breathtaking mathematical harmony. Newton and Einstein were not born into a chaotic void, but into a universe where nature follows elegant, discoverable patterns. From the titanic swirl of black holes to the subtle dance of subatomic quarks, reality is woven together by invariant physical laws.
A single, supreme, and infinitely wise Creator instituted these laws to sustain creation. His Will is not a erratic impulse, but an indomitable, unwavering foundation of order.

title: An unpredictable world
text:
Predictable Nonbelievers
Yet a curious paradox defines our world. Humans look out at the flawless regularity of nature, take its seamless stability for granted, and then ask: Why doesn’t God break the rules to prove He exists?
Many religious traditions eagerly rise to this demand, offering sacred texts filled with sensational suspensions of natural law. Unaware of the nightmare of the Pewniverse, millions fall prey to these miraculous fairy tales. But why is the human mind so seduced by the supernatural?
The answer lies deep within our psychological history:
First, the terrifying unpredictability of ancient nature—floods, plagues, and eclipses—instilled a profound helplessness in primitive humans. Desperate to survive, they sought to appease the unseen forces through sacrifices and rituals. In turn, manipulative priesthoods and despotic rulers exploited this fear, entrenching their authority over a fragile populace.
Second, millennia of this psychological conditioning have scarred the human subconscious. The concept of a quiet, law-abiding God feels unsatisfying—even repulsive—to a mind raised on fear. An invisible Creator who governs through steady, unyielding natural law lacks the sensational drama of a cosmic “Superman.”
The universe displays its infinite majesty every second, yet primitive intuition insists on a spectacle: How can we trust a Creator unless He proves His power by breaking His own rules?

“Who will believe in a God who does not part the Red Sea, induce virgin births, or teleport prophets across continents overnight?” cries the fearful, unconfident voice within us.

We remain fixated on what we want God to be, rather than perceiving what God reveals through His Creation—a cosmos operating through unwavering laws within a majestic physical order.
Sadly, the primitive mind still yearns for a Macho Deity wearing the crown of a king.
It is often said that “God created man in His own image.” But looking at human history, it would be truer to say: “Men created God in theirs.”

title: A God of miracles
text:
What truly constitutes a miracle?
By definition, it is an event that violates the immutable laws of nature — a human walking across liquid water without sinking, or stepping out of a roaring furnace completely unscathed.
If an empirical, physical cause can explain an event, it ceases to be a miracle. Walking across a frozen lake is not a supernatural marvel; it is simply the predictable mechanics of phase transitions and physical law.
With that distinction in mind, take a moment to reflect on a quiet, probing question:


Will you stop believing in God if He stops performing miracles?


Before answering, ask yourself: Who actually authored the laws of physics? Science does not create natural laws — it merely discovers them. Scientists observe recurring patterns across the cosmos and codify those observations using mathematical notation and conceptual frameworks. What we call “natural laws” are simply human descriptions of the Creator’s consistent, underlying order.
With this context established, let us examine three thought experiments that reframe how we view divine intervention:

The Sharpshooter in the Forest
Imagine an expert marksman taking aim at a deer in the woods. If he lowers his rifle and lets the deer leap safely into the brush, would you doubt his marksmanship, or would you wonder why he chose not to take the shot?
If the Creator created the universe from nothing, His power to manipulate physical matter is self-evident. The critical question is never whether He can suspend nature, but why He would choose to do so. Why would an omniscient Creator routinely break the cosmic rules He instituted?
Would performing localized miracles not be fundamentally unfair to the vast majority of humanity who were not present to witness them? Why should subsequent generations be expected to stake their existential conviction on ancient hearsay?
Furthermore, a localized miracle proves remarkably little. Even if you witnessed an inexplicable event firsthand, how could you objectively differentiate between a genuine breach of physical law and an extraordinarily sophisticated illusion? The boundary between mystery and sleight of hand is dangerously thin. And if firsthand experience can be doubted, how can second-hand testimony ever serve as bedrock evidence of truth for others?
The Disciplined Athlete
Consider an elite marathoner who begins her rigorous training routine at precisely 5:00 a.m. every single morning, rain or shine. Would you view her rigid schedule as a sign of robotic slavery to the clock, or would you admire her for her unwavering discipline, strength of will, and punctuality?
Why, then, do we question God’s Will simply because He chooses never to break the laws He established for the universe to follow? True strength of will does not bend to whim or fluctuate under pressure. The supreme Will is one that remains absolute, reliable, and unyielding. God’s indomitable Will is revealed not through chaotic interruptions, but through perfect consistency—causing apples to fall to the earth with flawless mathematical precision, time after time, millennium after millennium.
The Impartial Educator
Imagine a schoolteacher presiding over a classroom. Should she evaluate every student strictly and transparently according to a fair set of academic standards, or should she manipulate grades based on personal favoritism—passing students who flatter her while failing diligent students who score full marks but offer no praise?
If all human beings stand equal before their Creator, what higher standard could we demand than absolute, impartial justice? In a rational universe, every soul reaps precisely what it sows. Good deeds yield moral growth; wrongdoings carry their own inevitable decay. Flattery may deceive vulnerable human egos, but it holds no leverage over an all-Knowing, all-Seeing, and Just God.
The true grandeur of God’s consistent Will (ما شاءالله) lies in its complete impartiality. No individual can claim unfairness in a universe where the rules apply to all without exception.
Fire does not select whom to burn based on creed or prestige; gravity grants no exemptions to the pious. God’s original design for existence is flawless, operating with a perfection that requires no patch, no emergency override, and no miraculous intervention to correct a perceived imperfection.
